To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the phase of H I disturbances in the outskirts are sensitive to the azimuth of the dark perturber and that the asymmetry of the radial velocity at 180 l 0 is sensitive to the azimuth.
the perturbing sub-halo responsible for the observed H I disturbances is located at l = 50 l 10, b = 30 l 5, and that it has a mass ~1/100 that of the Milky way, and a periastron distance ~5 kpc.
we have developed a new method to infer the perturber location in Sun-centered coordinates from the tidal imprints on the outskirts of a galaxy's H I disk.
In summary, our research is concerned with
using the observed tidal disturbances on the outskirts the disk of our Galaxy to infer the properties of a dark perturbing satellite.
developing a method to characterize dark matter sub-halos by their tidal imprints on the outskirts of galaxies.
developing a new tool for characterizing the Milky Way and its satellite population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the observed planar asymmetries and disturbances in the H I disk of the Milky Way are likely the result of a tidal interaction with a perturbing sub-halo with a mass ~1/100th of the Milky way, and a perigalactic distance of ~5 – 10 kpc, and that the azimuth of the sub-halo is between –50°
the azimuthal location, pericentric distance, and mass of a perturbing sub-halo can be inferred from the analysis of its tidal imprints on the outskirts of H I disk of its primary galaxy.

our tidal analysis method is capable of determining the azimuth of the sub-halo perturber responsible, with a precision of ~30 degrees, and the mass and pericentric approach of the perturbing sub-halo to within an order of magnitude.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the tidal analysis method is a promising tool, which can be further developed to yield a more accurate characterization of perturbers.
we are able to constrain the perturber to a region between –50 l < 10.
the perturbing dark halo has an azimuth of ~–40 l –10.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the tidal analysis method of CB09 is a promising technique for characterizing the dark sub-haloes that are believed to be the primary building blocks of the dark matter haloes that host galaxies, and for potentially discovering new dwarf galaxies in the outer disk and halo of the Milky Way.
the tidal analysis method is potentially a viable tool for characterizing the dark perturber responsible, at least in part, for the H I disturbances on the outskirts.
the azimuth determination is relatively insensitive to uncertainties in the mass of the perturbing dark halo, and that the azimuth is the most reliable quantity to be inferred from this analysis.
